problem:
Given a list of integers nums and an integer k, return the k values that occur most often, in any order. The answer is guaranteed to be unique.

Example: nums = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], k = 2 -> [1, 2]
Example: nums = [4], k = 1 -> [4]

data.reference_solution:
from collections import Counter
from typing import List

def topKFrequent(nums: List[int], k: int) -> List[int]:
    count = Counter(nums)
    sorted_elements = sorted(count.keys(), key=lambda x: count[x], reverse=True)
    return sorted_elements[:k]
data.generator_code:
import random

def generate(rng, n):
    if n < 1:
        n = 1
    nums = [rng.randint(-100, 100) for _ in range(n)]
    unique_vals = list(set(nums))
    k = rng.randint(1, len(unique_vals))
    return [nums, k]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    if n < 1:
        n = 1
    nums = [i % (n // 2 + 1) for i in range(n)]
    unique_vals = list(set(nums))
    k = max(1, len(unique_vals) // 2)
    return [nums, k]

data.key_insight: The frequency of any element can be at most the total number of elements in the array (n). We can use an array of buckets where the index represents the frequency, and each bucket stores a list of elements that appear with that frequency.

steps.title: Initialize Buckets
steps.detail: Create an array of empty lists of size n + 1, where n is the length of nums. Index i will hold elements that appear i times.

steps.title: Populate Buckets
steps.detail: Iterate through the frequency map and place each number into the bucket corresponding to its frequency count.

steps.title: Collect Top K Elements
steps.detail: Traverse the buckets in reverse order (from highest frequency to lowest), appending elements to our result list until we have collected k elements.

data.checker_code:
def check(args, got, expected):
    nums, k = args
    import collections
    counts = collections.Counter(nums)
    sorted_unique = sorted(counts.keys(), key=lambda x: counts[x], reverse=True)
    expected_set = set(sorted_unique[:k])
    got_set = set(got)
    return got_set == expected_set and len(got) == k

data.pattern_summary: Use a hash map to tally frequencies or store state for quick O(1) lookups, avoiding nested scans of the input array.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We need to count frequencies of arbitrary values, which a hash map does efficiently.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers require ordered or contiguous data, whereas these values are scattered across the list.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Sliding windows deal with contiguous subarrays or sublists, not global element frequencies.

pattern_options.name: Binary search
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Binary search requires sorted data, and the input array is unsorted.

signals.hint: Implies you must track how many times each distinct element appears.
Implies you need a way to rank or select a subset based on those counts.

data.brute_force_idea: First, collect all unique numbers. Then, count the frequency of each unique number by scanning the entire input list again. Finally, sort the counts in descending order and take the first k elements.
data.brute_force_why: Counting each unique element takes O(n) time, and sorting the resulting list of unique elements takes O(u log u) time where u is the number of unique elements, leading to O(n log n) overall.
data.bottleneck: Scanning the entire nums array from scratch for every single unique element results in redundant iterations.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many times the inner loop runs relative to the outer loop.
Notice that we recount elements in nums repeatedly for every distinct value.
Ask yourself if you can collect all the counts in a single pass instead of rescanning.

data.overview: The Top K Frequent Elements algorithm finds the most common elements in an array using bucket sort. By mapping element frequencies to array indices, we avoid sorting and achieve linear time complexity.
data.intuition: Imagine organizing a closet by how often you wear your clothes. Instead of sorting every single item by exact preference, you put them into baskets labeled by the number of days you wear them: a basket for clothes worn once, twice, etc. Then, you simply grab items starting from the highest-frequency basket until you have k items.

data.insight: Instead of sorting elements by frequency using comparisons which takes O(n log n) time, we group elements into buckets indexed by their frequency. Since the maximum possible frequency of any element is n, an array of lists of size n+1 lets us place each element into its correct frequency bucket in linear time. We then collect elements starting from the highest frequency bucket down to 1 until we have collected k elements.

derivation.note: Counters builds the frequency map by iterating through nums once.
Initializes an array of empty lists of size n + 1.
Iterates through the unique elements in the count map.
Appends the number into its corresponding frequency bucket.
Iterates backwards through the frequency buckets from n down to 1.
Iterates through numbers inside the buckets, visiting each element at most once across all buckets.

data.time_summary: Lines 3, 4, 5, and 9-10 all scale linearly with the size of the input array n. The measured step counts scale predictably with n, confirming the linear O(n) time complexity.
data.space_summary: The space complexity is O(n) because we store the frequency map, the array of buckets of size n + 1, and the result array, all of which scale linearly with the number of unique elements and total elements.
data.takeaway: When items are bounded by a known numeric range like frequencies up to n, use bucket sort to bypass the O(n log n) comparison sorting bottleneck.
mistakes: Trying to sort the frequency dictionary directly using standard sorting algorithms instead of using positional buckets.
Allocating buckets of size n instead of n + 1, which causes an index out of bounds error when an element appears n times.
Forgetting to stop early once k elements have been gathered, which harms performance.
